beforeSession: Print the opening cards and choose a small stack that matches the writers' stamina for one sitting.
Set out pencils, blank paper, and a pencil cup as the shared idea holder.
Tell writers every opening must be fictional, invented, and broad enough that it does not reveal narrow real-world facts.
Preview the cards and remove any prompt that feels too close to an actual person or specific real-world detail.
Model one simple invented opening first: The green pencil leaned out of the cup and whispered, ____________________.
pencilCupOpeningSetup: Place five pencil colors in the cup and assign each one an opening job: first line, arrival, doorway, object, or question.
Let the adult draw the pencil so the activity stays guided and low-pressure.
Keep a small scrap pile beside the cup for false starts; writers may cross out and begin again without keeping every attempt.
Use invented labels on nearby slips, such as Cloud Hall, Button Market, Moon Desk, or Acorn Station.
Ask the writer to finish one opening stem before adding plot: Today the pencil cup held ____________________.
openingCoaching: Start with motion when a writer is stuck: The pencil rolled, pointed, tapped, slipped, or turned toward ____________________.
Ask for one clear noun before any explanation: Who or what appears first in the opening? ____________________.
Keep the first paragraph small: one sentence for the surprise, one sentence for the place, and one sentence for the first move.
When an opening sounds like a summary, ask the writer to move closer to the first moment: The first thing I noticed was ____________________.
For gentle revision, circle one word that can become more specific and replace it with an invented detail: ____________________.
privacyAndSafetyNotes: Use broad invented labels instead of narrow real-world facts.
Keep sharing limited to adult-led paper conversation.
Keep the activity paper-only and skip media capture.
Keep all characters fictional and avoid details that point to an actual writer.
Invite writers to skip any line they do not want to read aloud.
familyHandoff: Send along only the chosen slip and a blank page, not a log of the writer's full writing history.
Invite family adults to ask about the made-up beginning rather than correcting spelling first.
Suggest one adult-led line: My favorite invented detail was ____________________.
Remind family adults to keep narrow real-world facts and private routines off the story page.
Keep the handoff paper-only and adult-led.
reset: Return unused cards to the pack and recycle crossed-out scraps that contain narrow real-world facts.
Put the pencil colors back in the cup so the next session starts with the same simple choices.
Save only fictional examples that are useful for modeling future openings.
Check that take-home slips are blank except for invented story material.

openingRoutines.name: First Line Pencil Pull
openingRoutines.bestFor: Writers who need help getting the very first sentence onto the page.
steps: The adult draws one pencil and names its job: first line.
The writer chooses a fictional sound, color, or movement from the pencil cup.
The writer completes this line: The first sign that something was different was ____________________.
The adult asks the writer to add one more sentence showing who noticed it.

openingRoutines.name: Cup Character Arrival
openingRoutines.bestFor: Starting with a character before the setting is fully known.
steps: Choose one pencil and pretend it belongs to an invented character.
Ask what the character carries, wants, or misunderstands.
The writer completes this arrival line: Into the story came ____________________.
The adult prompts one first action, not a full backstory.

openingRoutines.name: Doorway Place Opening
openingRoutines.bestFor: Writers who like places, maps, rooms, and entrances.
steps: Place a folded blank slip beside the pencil cup and call it a doorway.
Name an invented place that could fit behind it.
The writer completes this opening: Behind the pencil cup doorway was ____________________.
The adult asks for one detail the character sees before stepping in.

openingRoutines.name: Object Invitation Start
openingRoutines.bestFor: Turning ordinary desk objects into story starters.
steps: Pick one paper-only object near the cup, such as an eraser, paperclip, ruler, or index card.
Ask what the object seems to invite the character to do.
The writer completes this line: The object on the desk seemed to be inviting ____________________.
The adult asks the writer to write the first yes, no, or maybe response.

openingRoutines.name: Opening Question Card
openingRoutines.bestFor: Writers who start faster when there is a mystery but no scary content.
steps: The adult chooses a card and turns its prompt into a gentle question.
The writer answers with an invented place, object, or character.
The writer completes this question opening: Why was ____________________ waiting in the pencil cup?
The adult reminds the writer not to solve the whole question yet.

openingRoutines.name: First Move Revision
openingRoutines.bestFor: Improving a plain beginning without rewriting the whole page.
steps: The writer underlines the first sentence of a draft opening.
The adult asks which word can become more vivid, specific, or surprising.
The writer rewrites only that sentence using this stem: This time, the opening begins with ____________________.
The adult has the writer compare both versions and choose the one that starts the story faster.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: The Tapping Pencil
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Write a fictional opening where a pencil taps three times before anything happens: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask which invented sound should come next: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: New Pencil in the Cup
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Begin with a new pencil appearing in the cup and invent who placed it there: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask what the made-up visitor wants without using a narrow real-world fact: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: Door Behind the Cup
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Start with a tiny doorway opening behind the pencil cup and name the invented place beyond it: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask for one fictional detail seen through the doorway: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: The Object That Asked
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Choose an ordinary paper-table object and write an opening where it asks for help: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask what the character does first with the object: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: Question on the Label
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Invent a label on the pencil cup that asks a question no one expected: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask which word on the invented label matters most: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: First Move
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Begin with a character making one small move toward the pencil cup: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask what the move shows about the character: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: Color Pencil Weather
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Write a fictional opening where the color of a pencil changes the mood of an invented place: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask which color belongs in the first sentence: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: Eraser Map
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Start with an eraser revealing a pretend map that does not match any narrow real-world place detail: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask what invented landmark appears first: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: Ruler Edge Door
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Begin with a ruler edge becoming the line between an ordinary desk and an invented world: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask what waits on the fictional far side: ____________________.

takeHomeOpeningSlips.title: Sharper Opening
takeHomeOpeningSlips.direction: Rewrite a plain opening by adding one specific invented object from the pencil cup: ____________________.
takeHomeOpeningSlips.familyLine: Ask which version starts faster and why: ____________________.

optionalSharePrompts: Read only the first sentence you want to share: ____________________.
Point to the invented word that made the opening feel alive: ____________________.
Share the fictional object that starts the story, without narrow real-world facts: ____________________.
Tell the group what the character notices first: ____________________.
Share the made-up place name from your opening: ____________________.
Read the opening question and stop before the answer: ____________________.
Name one word you revised to make the beginning clearer: ____________________.
Tell a family adult which pencil-cup idea you would use again: ____________________.
